introduction: These hundred readings are ‘Abdu’l-Bahá speaking of his own life: a childhood of illness, mobs and a father in chains; exile from city to city; decades in a prison town where he slept on a mat and was happy; journeys through Europe and America in old age; days with no hour to himself, and letters written at dawn or late at night to friends far away. Most are recollections taken down by others. The passages set beside them come from other lives of service told in the first person or by those who watched, above all Paul's letters, with Moses, Elijah, Job and the Psalms, Thoreau and Tennyson's Ulysses. A few ask questions of such a life: Pascal on staying in one's room, Seneca on crowds, Jethro on burdens carried alone, the lotos-eaters on rest.
questions: Many of these memories are of small things: a meal in a poor man's house, a mat for a bed, a cushion in Paris. What do the small details tell you that a list of achievements would not?
He says he was happy in prison. Reading Lovelace and Byron beside him, what do you think makes that possible?
Jethro warned Moses that he would wear away carrying everything alone. How do the readings show the cost of a life given to others, and how was it borne?
Paul and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá both write to distant friends with great warmth. What part has letter-writing, or its modern forms, played in holding your own friendships together?
Tennyson's Ulysses will not rust unburnished in old age. What work do you hope still to be doing late in life?
Which single recollection here would you most want to retell to someone else, and why?

outside.why: Jesus watched a poor widow throw two mites into the treasury and said that she had cast in more than all the rich.
Abraham ran from his tent door to meet three strangers in the heat of the day and begged them to rest and eat.
The Sayings of the Fathers call excellent the study of Torah when it is combined with a worldly occupation.
The widow of Zarephath had only a handful of meal and a little oil, and made a cake of it for a stranger first.
Paul asks the Romans to rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
Jesus said that he that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much.
The Qur’an says that God commands you to restore deposits to their owners, and to judge justly between people.
Jesus said: the foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.
The Letter to the Hebrews says of the faithful of old that they confessed they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
Pascal traced all the unhappiness of men to one fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber. What can a life of exile teach that a settled life cannot?
Plato held that rhythm and harmony find their way into the inward places of the soul.
Asked whose fault a man's blindness was, Jesus answered: neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents, but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.
The Letter to the Hebrews remembers those who were stoned, who wandered about destitute, afflicted, tormented.
William Blake asked how a child, when fears annoy, can do other than droop his tender wing and forget his youthful spring. What kept a childhood spent among mobs and prisons from being only a wound?
Job, stripped of everything in a day, said: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.
The Letter to the Hebrews recalls believers who took joyfully the spoiling of their goods, knowing they had a better substance.
Luke says of the boy Jesus that he increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.
Genesis says that Joseph was put into the prison where the king's prisoners were bound, but the Lord was with Joseph.
Oscar Wilde wrote of a prisoner who looked with a wistful eye upon that little tent of blue which prisoners call the sky. What does a child carry away from seeing a parent in such a place?
The exiles by the rivers of Babylon sat down and wept when they remembered Zion.
The psalmist says: if I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there shall Thy hand lead me.
Elijah, alone on the mountain, found that the Lord was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, and then heard a still small voice.
The first letter of Peter says: think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you.
Paul observed that he that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, and he that is married for the things of the world. Is a life of service better lived alone or in a family?
Tobias prays on his wedding night, recalling the words: it is not good that man should be alone.
Jesus told his disciples that when they were brought before kings and rulers he would give them a mouth and wisdom.
Socrates told his judges: men of Athens, I honour and love you, but I shall obey God rather than you.
Elijah said: I have been very jealous for the Lord, and I, even I only, am left, and they seek my life.
Milton wrote of the seraph Abdiel: faithful found among the faithless, faithful only he.
The psalm says: some trust in chariots, and some in horses, but we will remember the name of the Lord our God.
In the prison at Philippi, at midnight, Paul and Silas prayed and sang praises, and the prisoners heard them.
Thoreau wrote that a man is rich in proportion to the number of things which he can afford to let alone.
Paul says: I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
Jesus said: consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin.
Seneca wrote that it is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor. How quickly do comforts become needs, and how is the habit unlearned?
Richard Lovelace wrote from prison that stone walls do not a prison make, nor iron bars a cage.
Byron's prisoner of Chillon says that his very chains and he grew friends, and that he regained his freedom with a sigh. Is joy in prison a kind of freedom, or only a long habit?
Ruth said: intreat me not to leave thee; whither thou goest, I will go, and where thou lodgest, I will lodge.
Jesus said of his hearers that seeing they see not, and hearing they hear not.
Tennyson's Ulysses says: how dull it is to pause, to make an end, to rust unburnished, not to shine in use.
Paul lists his travels: in journeyings often, in perils of waters, in weariness and painfulness, and beside these the care of all the churches.
Tennyson's old voyager says: I am a part of all that I have met.
Thoreau called the inventions of his day pretty toys, improved means to an unimproved end. What might a visitor from a prison city have found amusing in the electric signs of Broadway?
Shakespeare ends a sonnet of regrets: but if the while I think on thee, dear friend, all losses are restored and sorrows end.
Paul writes to people he has not yet met: I long to see you, that I may be comforted together with you.
Paul tells the Philippians: God is my record, how greatly I long after you all.
Emerson wrote that a friend is a person with whom I may be sincere; before him I may think aloud.
Thoreau kept three chairs in his house: one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society.
Jesus said: when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind. What should a guest of honour notice at the tables of the notable?
Seneca advised his friend to avoid crowds, since he never came home from them the same man. What allowed someone pursued by crowds and photographers to stay himself?
Paul heard the answer: my strength is made perfect in weakness; and said: when I am weak, then am I strong.
Isaiah says that God giveth power to the faint, and that they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength.
Paul says that we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God.
Jeremiah says that the word was as a burning fire shut up in his bones, and he could not stay.
Whitman saw the purpose of his age in the earth spanned, the oceans crossed, the distant brought near.
Jesus told his disciples to say, when they had done all: we are unprofitable servants. Why do those who have done most speak of having done nothing?
Paul said on his way to Jerusalem that he did not count his life dear, so that he might finish his course with joy.
Paul says that though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
Paul reminds the Thessalonians that he was gentle among them as a nurse, labouring night and day.
Tennyson's lotos-eaters plead: let us alone; is there any peace in ever climbing up the climbing wave? What answers the wish to rest, in a body that is worn out?
The elder writes that he will not write with ink and pen, but trusts shortly to see his friend and speak face to face.
At the grave of his friend Lazarus, Jesus wept, and those who saw it said: behold how he loved him.
The psalm asks: so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
The first letter to Timothy asks prayers for all that are in authority. What place do friendly dealings with governors and judges have in the life of one they hold prisoner?
Jesus said: render unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's, and unto God the things that are God's.
Isaiah says that the wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad, and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
Proverbs says that as cold waters to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country.
By the Sea of Galilee Jesus said to two fishermen: follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.
Wordsworth wrote that the world is too much with us; getting and spending, we lay waste our powers.
Thoreau went to the woods because he wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life.
Jesus told of a man who made a great supper and bade many.
The Qur’an says: there are above you guardians, generous and recording, who know all that ye do.
Omar Khayyam wrote that the moving finger writes, and having writ, moves on, and not a line can be cancelled. How would you live if everything you said were being written down?
The psalmist says: I am weary with my groaning; all the night I water my couch with my tears.
Peter quoted the prophet Joel: your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams.
Jesus said: let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth. Why would a person keep hidden the practices that most sustain him?
Paul says: I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord.
The psalm says: behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
Paul describes his life: as sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.
The Letter to the Hebrews pictures the living as compassed about with a great cloud of witnesses.
Mark says that there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
Moses said: I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me.
Jethro told Moses: the thing that thou doest is not good; thou wilt surely wear away; thou art not able to perform it thyself alone. When should one who carries a community's burdens share them?
Jesus said to Martha, careful and troubled about many things, that one thing is needful. How does a person drowned in occupations keep hold of the one thing?
Jesus said: I must work while it is day; the night cometh, when no man can work.
The Preacher says: whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might.
Jesus said: come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Lamentations says that the Lord's compassions fail not; they are new every morning.
Paul tells the Corinthians: ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men.
Paul tells the Thessalonians that he was taken from them in presence, not in heart.
The psalmist prays: now also when I am old and greyheaded, O God, forsake me not, until I have shewed Thy strength unto this generation.
The psalm says that God knoweth our frame; He remembereth that we are dust.
Tennyson's Ulysses says that old age hath yet his honour and his toil, and some work of noble note may yet be done.
Shakespeare speaks of that time of year when yellow leaves, or none, or few, do hang upon the boughs. What does age take from a servant of others, and what does it give?
Tennyson's old sailors are made weak by time and fate, but strong in will to strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.
Paul says near his end: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.
In John's Gospel Jesus says: I have finished the work which Thou gavest me to do.
When Paul took leave at Miletus they all wept sore, sorrowing most that they should see his face no more.
John's Gospel says of Jesus that having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end.
Longfellow wrote that lives of great men remind us we can make our lives sublime, and leave footprints on the sands of time. What does a remembered life ask of those who remember it?

corinthians-in-perils.text: In journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers, in perils by mine own countrymen, in perils by the heathen, in perils in the city, in perils in the wilderness, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brethren; In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness. Beside those things that are without, that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches

acts-finish-my-course-with-joy.text: And now, behold, I go bound in the spirit unto Jerusalem, not knowing the things that shall befall me there: Save that the Holy Ghost witnesseth in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions abide me. But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God

corinthians-strength-made-perfect-in-wea.text: My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me. Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong

thessalonians-labouring-night-and-day.text: But we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children: So being affectionately desirous of you, we were willing to have imparted unto you, not the gospel of God

kings-handful-of-meal.text: As the Lord thy God liveth, I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die. And Elijah said unto her, Fear not; go and do as thou hast said: but make me thereof a little cake first, and bring it unto me, and after make for thee and for thy son. For thus saith the Lord God of Israel, The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the Lord sendeth rain upon the earth. And she went and did according to the saying of Elijah: and she, and he, and her house, did eat many days

mark-no-leisure-so-much-as-to-eat.text: Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat

numbers-not-able-to-bear-alone.text: I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me

john-finished-the-work.text: I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do

philippians-long-after-you-all.text: For God is my record, how greatly I long after you all in the bowels of Jesus Christ

matthew-foxes-have-holes.text: The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head

hebrews-spoiling-of-your-goods.text: For ye had compassion of me in my bonds, and took joyfully the spoiling of your goods, knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance

corinthians-unmarried-careth.text: He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord: But he that is married careth for the things that are of the world, how he may please his wife

luke-mouth-and-wisdom.text: they shall lay their hands on you, and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues, and into prisons, being brought before kings and rulers for my name's sake. And it shall turn to you for a testimony. Settle it therefore in your hearts, not to meditate before what ye shall answer: For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist

psalm-when-i-am-old.text: O God, thou hast taught me from my youth: and hitherto have I declared thy wondrous works. Now also when I am old and greyheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come

john-loved-them-unto-the-end.text: having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end

corinthians-epistle-written-in-our-heart.text: Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men

john-epistle-paper-and-ink.text: I had many things to write, but I will not with ink and pen write unto thee: But I trust I shall shortly see thee, and we shall speak face to face

tennyson-part-of-all-that-i-have-met.text: I am a part of all that I have met
tennyson-part-of-all-that-i-have-met.author: Alfred Tennyson

tennyson-to-rust-unburnished.author: Alfred Tennyson

tennyson-old-age-hath-yet-his-honour.text: Old age hath yet his honour and his toil; / Death closes all: but something ere the end, / Some work of noble note, may yet be done
tennyson-old-age-hath-yet-his-honour.author: Alfred Tennyson

tennyson-to-strive-to-seek.text: much is taken, much abides; and tho' / We are not now that strength which in old days / Moved earth and heaven; that which we are, we are; / One equal temper of heroic hearts, / Made weak by time and fate, but strong in will / To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield
tennyson-to-strive-to-seek.author: Alfred Tennyson

quran-noble-recorders.text: Lo! there are above you guardians, Generous and recording, Who know (all) that ye do
